guide.title: Sugarbush Resort, Vermont: Lincoln Peak, Mount Ellen, and the Mad River Valley
guide.intro: Damon and Sara Gadd purchased the Ulla Lodge in December 1952, and in spring 1957 Damon Gadd applied for a lease of National Forest land on Lincoln Peak to develop a ski area; construction commenced April 28, 1958, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page. In 1958, Damon Gadd and Jack Murphy founded Sugarbush Ski Area on the northeast side of Lincoln Peak in the town of Warren; a three-seat gondola was installed that was, at the time, the nation's longest lift, per Wikipedia's "Warren, Vermont" article. Sugarbush's original 1958-59 lift infrastructure was a 9,300-foot gondola with 88 three-person cabins imported from Italy, plus a novice T-bar; the gondola likely opened December 27, 1958, a few days after the T-bar's debut, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page.

sections.heading: Castlerock, Glen Ellen, and "Mascara Mountain"
sections.body: For the 1959-60 season, a new Carlevaro & Savio double chairlift was installed on the peak that became known as Castlerock, which quickly developed a reputation for excellent expert skiing, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page. The Valley House Double chairlift was installed for the 1960-61 season, giving lower-level skiers access via a new, wider trail named Snowball. In February 1962, Walter Elliott announced initial financing and land options to develop a separate ski area north of Sugarbush, on Mount Ellen and General Stark Mountain, which became Glen Ellen. On May 1, 1964, Sugarbush announced that world champion racer Stein Eriksen had been hired as its next ski school director (correcting the finder's account, which treated this as Eriksen's arrival date rather than his hiring announcement); a Village Double chairlift was added for the 1964-65 season to accompany the expansion. The 2013-14 season was marketed as Mount Ellen's 50th anniversary and Sugarbush's 55th, dating Glen Ellen/Mount Ellen's opening to approximately 1963-64, per Wikipedia's Sugarbush Resort article.

sections.heading: Accidents and losses in the 1960s and 1970s
sections.body: On April 3, 1963, Sugarbush ski school director Peter Estin was found dead in his hotel room at age 35, leaving four children, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page. On January 14, 1964, Sugarbush ski shop owner Sig Buchmayr, 57, was killed in a car accident in Hopewell Junction, New York. On February 27, 1965, a grip on Sugarbush's gondola loosened and a cabin fell an estimated 18 feet, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page, hospitalizing two passengers. On December 15, 1972, the summit terminal of Sugarbush's gondola was destroyed by fire.

sections.heading: Ownership, from the Gadds to Alterra
sections.body: The Gadds sold Sugarbush in 1977 for a reported $4.2 million to Roy Cohen, operating through his company Solon Automated Services, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page. In the late 1970s, Solon Automated Services purchased the separate Glen Ellen ski area for a reported $2.4 million and renamed it Sugarbush North. ARA Services Inc. (later Aramark) acquired Solon Automated Services and Sugarbush following the 1982-83 season, owning it from 1983 to 1986. Claneil Enterprises purchased Sugarbush from ARA Services in 1986 for $14.5 million and transformed it into a four-season resort facility, owning it until 1994. In October 1994, Les Otten's LBO Resort Enterprises Corp. purchased Sugarbush from Claneil Enterprises for $9.1 million, and in 1996 LBO Resort Enterprises was rolled into American Skiing Company. Under American Skiing Company's ownership, Sugarbush received seven new lifts and a 300% expansion of snowmaking capacity, according to Wikipedia's Sugarbush Resort article. In October 2001, Summit Ventures NE, Inc., headed by Win Smith (son of Merrill Lynch partner Winthrop H. Smith Sr.), purchased Sugarbush from American Skiing Company; Smith moved to Vermont full-time and took over day-to-day management of the resort in 2004, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page. On November 14, 2019, Win Smith announced the sale of Sugarbush Resort to Denver-based Alterra Mountain Company, with the sale price kept private; Alterra CEO Rusty Gregory said, "Their local strategy and tactics, and our large platform and larger-scale business model, I think, will make a great combination," per NBC Boston's November 14, 2019 report. The acquisition closed in January 2020.

sections.heading: Lifts since 1995
sections.body: For the 1995-96 season, four new quad chairlifts were installed, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page: the Slide Brook Express, Gatehouse Express, Super Bravo Express, and North Ridge Express, plus the North Lynx Triple, in what the source calls the single biggest off-season lift transformation in modern ski resort history. The Slide Brook Express, built in 1995 to link Sugarbush's Lincoln Peak (South) and Mount Ellen (North) sections by lift for the first time, is a 3.4-kilometer four-seater chairlift described as the world's longest chairlift, according to Neilson Active Holidays. The legendary Castlerock Double chairlift was replaced for the 2001-02 season, and a new Green Mountain Express was installed for 2002-03. The Valley House Double was replaced with a quad chairlift for the 2015-16 season, and the Village and Sunnyside double chairlifts were replaced with quads for 2017-18. The Heaven's Gate Triple chairlift, originally installed in 1984-85, was replaced with a fixed-grip quad for the 2024-25 season.

sections.heading: In Warren
sections.body: The Pitcher Inn is located at the heart of the village of Warren, Vermont, at 275 Main Street, per the inn's own website. Warren Store operates as a country store, deli, and bakery at 284 Main Street, selling coffee, grill items, baked goods, and local Vermont products, with a second-floor boutique offering clothing, jewelry, and housewares, per the store's own website. The Warren Covered Bridge, a queen-post-truss wooden bridge over the Mad River built by Walter Bagley, was added to the National Register of Historic Places on August 7, 1974; it is one of only two remaining bridges in Vermont whose trusses are covered on both the inside and the outside, and it sustained abutment damage during Hurricane Irene in 2011 but remained open to traffic, according to Wikipedia's "Warren Covered Bridge" article.

faq.question: Who owns Sugarbush now?
faq.answer: Sugarbush has been owned by Alterra Mountain Company since an acquisition from Win Smith's ownership group closed in January 2020, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page. Smith had announced the sale on November 14, 2019.

faq.question: Is Sugarbush one mountain or two?
faq.answer: Sugarbush spans two connected areas, Lincoln Peak and Mount Ellen (originally the separate Glen Ellen ski area), linked by the Slide Brook Express chairlift built in 1995, per New England Ski History's Sugarbush history page.
